items.prompt: What is the name of the core part of an operating system that runs with full hardware privileges?

options.label: Kernel
Shell
Bootloader
Compiler

rubric: The kernel is the privileged core of the OS.
The shell is a user-level command interface, not the privileged core.

items.prompt: What is a process?

options.label: A block of RAM reserved for a program
An executable file saved on the disk
A program that is currently running
A command that a user types in a shell

rubric: A process is a running instance of a program.
A program file on disk is not yet a process.

items.prompt: Which component of the OS decides which ready process gets the CPU next?

options.label: Scheduler
Page table
File system
Device driver

rubric: The scheduler picks the next process to run.
Page tables map memory addresses, not CPU time.

items.prompt: What is a system call?

options.label: A call from one user function to another in a program
A request from a program to the kernel for a service
A message that a program sends to another computer
A signal that the hardware sends to restart the system

rubric: System calls are how programs ask the kernel for services.
Ordinary function calls do not enter the kernel.

items.prompt: What does the term 'virtual memory' refer to?

options.label: A copy of the whole disk that the kernel keeps in RAM
An abstraction giving each process its own address space
A small, fast cache built into the CPU to speed up loads
A memory region the kernel reserves for the shell to run in

rubric: Virtual memory gives each process a private address space.
It is not a CPU cache.

items.prompt: Which of the following are typical process states in an OS? Select all that apply.

options.label: Compiled
Running
Ready
Installed

items.prompt: A student reads that the OS stores files in named units arranged in directories on a disk. She wants the name of the OS component responsible for this organisation. Which one is it?

options.label: File system
Scheduler
Interrupt handler
Memory manager

rubric: The file system organises files and directories on storage.
The memory manager handles RAM, not files.

items.prompt: Why do operating systems separate user mode from kernel mode?

options.label: To stop programs from reading or writing any memory outside the kernel's own
To make programs run faster by skipping hardware checks on trusted code
To stop ordinary programs from directly using privileged hardware operations
To let users edit kernel code safely while the system is still running

rubric: Privilege separation protects the system from faulty or hostile programs.
Mode separation adds protection, not speed.

items.prompt: What does a context switch accomplish?

options.label: Moves a running process from user mode into kernel mode so it can make a system call
Copies a process's open files and working directory to a new process it has created
Saves one process's CPU state and loads another's so the CPU can change tasks
Erases a paused process's memory pages so that other processes can use the freed space

rubric: A context switch saves and restores CPU state between processes.
It does not delete memory or move files.

items.prompt: Why can a computer with 8 GB of RAM run programs whose combined memory needs exceed 8 GB?

options.label: The OS compresses every program to about half its size when loading it
Pages not currently in use can be moved to disk
The CPU keeps the overflow data in its registers and caches
Programs are made to share one copy of memory without isolation

rubric: Virtual memory swaps or pages unused data to disk.
Registers are far too small to hold the overflow.

items.prompt: In round-robin scheduling, what happens when a process uses up its time slice?

options.label: It goes to the back of the ready queue and another process runs
It stays at the front of the ready queue and runs again after a short pause
It is blocked until every other process in the queue has finished running
It is swapped out to disk and must be reloaded by the user to continue

rubric: Round-robin preempts at the end of a quantum and requeues the process.
It does not kill the process or let it run to completion.

items.prompt: Why does a program that wants to read a file call the kernel rather than touching the disk itself?

options.label: Programs run too slowly to talk to hardware directly
Only the kernel can hold file data, since programs keep none
The disk accepts requests from just one program at a time
The kernel controls device access and enforces permissions

rubric: The kernel mediates device access for safety and sharing.
Disks are not restricted to boot-time reads.

items.prompt: Which statements correctly explain what a device driver does? Select all that apply.

options.label: It lets the OS support many different devices through a common interface
It replaces the need for the kernel to manage the device
It translates generic OS requests into commands for specific hardware
It schedules which user process runs next

rubric: Drivers adapt hardware specifics to a common OS interface.
Scheduling is the scheduler's job, and drivers work with the kernel rather than replacing it.

items.prompt: A user opens a text editor and a browser at the same time on a single-core computer. Both appear to run smoothly together. Which explanation best describes why?

options.label: The browser is paused until the editor closes
The OS rapidly switches the CPU between the two processes
The editor runs inside the browser's memory and shares its CPU time
Each process gets its own dedicated CPU core to run on

rubric: Time-slicing gives the illusion of simultaneous execution.
A single core cannot dedicate itself to each process.

items.prompt: Which statement correctly distinguishes a program from a process?

options.label: A program is the part of the OS that executes code; a process is the file of instructions stored on disk
A program runs in kernel mode with full access; a process always runs in user mode with restrictions
A program is a file of instructions on disk; a process is a running instance with its own memory and state
A program uses a single thread of execution; a process is any program that uses more than one thread

rubric: A process is a program in execution, with its own address space and state; a program is passive code on disk.
Distractors confuse the roles of program and OS, or mix up the distinction with threads and privilege modes.

items.prompt: Why does a user program use a system call to write data to a disk file?

options.label: It makes the code run faster by skipping the scheduler and driving the hardware directly from user mode
It lets the compiler check types and library calls before the program is allowed to start running
It asks the kernel to perform a privileged operation, such as device access, on the program's behalf
It copies the program into memory so that the loader can execute its first instruction on the CPU

rubric: User code cannot touch devices directly; system calls are the controlled entry into the kernel.
Distractors confuse system calls with performance tricks, loading, or compile-time checking.

items.prompt: What is the main job of a process's page table?

options.label: It records the CPU registers saved when a process is paused
It lists which processes are ready to run and in what order
It stores the directories and files kept on a disk partition
It maps virtual pages to physical frames in RAM

rubric: The page table translates virtual page numbers to physical frame numbers.
Distractors describe the ready queue, the file system, and the saved context.

items.prompt: A process has issued a read request to a slow disk and cannot continue until the data arrives. In which state is it?

options.label: Running
Terminated
Ready
Blocked (waiting)

rubric: A process waiting for I/O is blocked and not eligible for the CPU until the I/O completes.
Ready means it could run right now; running means it is on the CPU.

items.prompt: What happens during a context switch between two processes?

options.label: The kernel saves the running process's CPU state and restores the saved state of another process
The CPU is restarted so that both processes begin again from their first instruction in order
The kernel deletes the first process's memory and then loads the second program from disk again
The kernel merges both address spaces so the two processes can run on the CPU at the same moment

rubric: A context switch saves registers and the program counter of one process and restores those of the next.
Distractors imagine memory being wiped, processes restarting, or address spaces merging.

items.prompt: Which statements correctly describe benefits or properties of virtual memory? Select all that apply.

options.label: A program can use more memory than fits in RAM because some pages can be kept on disk
Each process gets its own private address space, isolating it from other processes
Every memory access becomes faster than direct access to physical memory
Page faults can never occur once a process has started running
Two processes can never share any physical memory

rubric: Virtual memory provides isolation and lets less-used pages live on disk.
Page faults do occur, translation adds work, and shared libraries do share physical frames.

items.prompt: A user runs a text tool that waits for keystrokes. While it waits, a video player on the same single-core machine keeps playing smoothly. Why can the video player keep running?

options.label: The keyboard driver runs the video player's code while the tool waits for the next key
The waiting tool is blocked, so the scheduler gives the CPU to ready processes such as the video player
The tool was terminated and the OS restarts it again each time a key is pressed
The waiting tool keeps spinning on the CPU, but the kernel gives the video player a faster clock speed

rubric: A process waiting for input is blocked and consumes no CPU, so the scheduler runs other ready processes.
Distractors assume busy-waiting, drivers running user code, or restart-on-keypress behaviour.

items.prompt: Processes A, B and C arrive at time 0 in that order with CPU bursts of 6, 3 and 5 ms. Round-robin scheduling uses a 4 ms quantum and ignores switch cost. At what time does B finish?

options.label: 9 ms
7 ms
11 ms
3 ms

rubric: A runs 0-4, then B runs 4-7 and completes its 3 ms burst.
3 ms ignores A's turn; other values come from misordering the queue.

items.prompt: A system uses 4 KB pages (4096 bytes). Into which page number and offset does virtual address 10000 fall?

options.label: Page 3, offset 1808
Page 1, offset 5904
Page 2, offset 1904
Page 2, offset 1808

rubric: Distractors use a wrong quotient or a wrong remainder.

items.prompt: A C program runs `fork(); fork(); printf("hi\n");` and every fork succeeds. How many times is "hi" printed in total?
rubric: The first fork gives 2 processes and the second doubles it to 4; each prints once.
2 and 3 undercount the second fork in the child; 8 assumes three forks.

items.prompt: File `report.txt` is owned by alice, group dev, with mode 640 (rw-r-----). Bob is in group dev but is not the owner. What can Bob do with the file?

options.label: Read it, because the group class has r but no w
Neither, because only the owner may open the file at all
Modify it, because group members share the owner's write right
Read and modify it, because membership in dev gives full access

rubric: Mode 640 gives the group read only; Bob uses the group class.
Distractors assume group inherits write, full access, or no access at all.

items.prompt: Jobs with CPU bursts of 8, 4 and 2 ms all arrive at time 0. A non-preemptive shortest-job-first scheduler runs them. What is the average waiting time?
rubric: Order 2, 4, 8 gives waits 0, 2, 6, so the average is 8/3 = 2.67 ms.
6.67 ms is the FIFO result for the order 8, 4, 2.

items.prompt: Which of these operations in a user program require a system call? Select all that apply.

options.label: Adding two integers held in local variables
Comparing two values in a loop condition
Creating a new process with `fork`
Opening a file on disk with `open`
Calling a function you defined in the same program

rubric: Opening files and creating processes need kernel services.
Arithmetic, local function calls and comparisons run entirely in user mode.

items.prompt: A process has 3 physical frames, all empty at the start, and uses FIFO page replacement. It references pages in this order: 1, 2, 3, 1, 4, 2. How many page faults occur?
rubric: Faults on 1, 2, 3 and 4 (evicting 1); the second 1 hits and 2 still hits, giving 4.
5 or 6 assume extra faults on pages still in memory; 3 ignores page 4.

items.prompt: A system uses 32-bit virtual addresses and 4 KB pages. What are the page number and offset of virtual address `0x00403A7C`?

options.label: Page `0x403`, offset `0xA7C`
Page `0x40`, offset `0x3A7C`
Page `0x403A7`, offset `0xC`
Page `0x403A`, offset `0x7C`

rubric: 4 KB pages need a 12-bit offset, which is the last three hex digits, so the page number is the remaining upper bits.
Distractors split at the wrong bit boundary, ignoring that 12 bits equal 3 hex digits.

items.prompt: Processes A, B and C arrive at time 0 in that order with CPU bursts of 5, 3 and 2 ms. Round-robin uses a 2 ms quantum and ignores switch cost. At what time does B finish?

options.label: 10 ms
9 ms
8 ms
7 ms

rubric: Timeline: A 0-2, B 2-4, C 4-6 (done), A 6-8, B 8-9 (done), A 9-10, so B finishes at 9 ms.
Other values come from skipping a rotation or ending B's last slice early.

items.prompt: A TLB lookup costs 10 ns and a memory access costs 100 ns. The system has a single-level page table and a 90% TLB hit ratio. What is the effective memory access time?

options.label: 110 ns
100 ns
120 ns
130 ns

rubric: Other values ignore the TLB lookup time or the extra page-table access on a miss.

items.prompt: What does this C code print, counting the total number of `x` characters written by all processes? `pid_t p = fork(); if (p == 0) fork(); putchar('x');` Assume fork succeeds.
rubric: The parent forks once; only the child forks again, giving 3 processes in total, and each prints one x.
Choosing 4 assumes both parent and child fork a second time; 2 ignores the child's fork.

items.prompt: Which command line writes both standard output and standard error of `cmd` into the file `log` in a POSIX shell?

options.label: `cmd | log 2>&1`
`cmd 2>&1 > log`
`cmd 2> log`
`cmd > log 2>&1`

rubric: Redirections apply left to right: stdout goes to the file first, then stderr is duplicated onto the same destination.
With `2>&1 > log`, stderr is duplicated onto the terminal before stdout is redirected, so it never reaches the file.

items.prompt: A program takes several locks in varying order and occasionally deadlocks. Which changes remove one of the necessary conditions for deadlock? Select all that apply.

options.label: Raise the priority of threads that have been waiting the longest
Use trylock and release held locks on failure, then retry later
Make each thread request all its needed locks together before running
Add more CPU cores so lock holders finish their work sooner
Require every thread to acquire locks in one fixed global order

rubric: Fixed ordering breaks circular wait, requesting all at once breaks hold-and-wait, and trylock with release allows rollback of held locks.
Priority and more cores change timing but leave all four deadlock conditions intact.

items.prompt: A student simulates FIFO page replacement with 3 physical frames, starting empty. The reference string is 1,2,3,4,1,2,5,1,2,3,4,5. She counts every reference that is not already in memory as a page fault. How many page faults occur?
rubric: Faults occur on 1,2,3,4,1,2,5,3,4, which is 9; the references to 1, 2 and the final 5 hit.
Counts of 10 or 8 come from mis-tracking which page FIFO evicts.

items.prompt: `time ./job` reports real 12.0s, user 0.4s and sys 0.2s on an otherwise idle machine. Which diagnosis fits best?

options.label: The job was running in kernel mode the whole time, making system calls that are not counted as sys time
The job is CPU-bound, but the shell under-reports user time for programs that run longer than ten seconds
The job spent most of its time blocked, for example waiting on disk or network I/O
The scheduler gave the job a small CPU share because many other busy processes were competing for cores

rubric: Real time far exceeds user plus sys, and the machine is idle, so the job was off the CPU, most likely blocked on I/O.
Distractors assume CPU work that the accounting would show, or contention that an idle machine rules out.

items.prompt: After a team raises concurrent worker processes on one host from 8 to 24, CPU utilisation drops, disk activity spikes and throughput falls. What is the most likely cause?

options.label: The TLB is too small for 24 processes, so every memory access now needs a full page-table walk
The combined working sets exceed physical memory, so processes spend their time servicing page faults
The scheduler quantum is too long, so each process holds the CPU while the other workers wait idle
Disk fragmentation grew because more processes are writing files, which slows every read and write

rubric: Falling CPU use with rising disk activity after adding processes signals thrashing: working sets no longer fit in RAM.
Quantum, TLB and fragmentation effects would not produce a sharp disk spike with idle CPU.

items.prompt: A process shows state `Z` in `ps`. An admin runs `kill -9` on its PID, but the entry stays. Why?

options.label: It has already exited; the entry remains until its parent calls `wait()` to collect the exit status
The kernel keeps zombies alive to hold their open files until the next periodic cleanup pass
It is blocked in uninterruptible disk I/O, so the signal stays queued until the read completes
SIGKILL is ignored by children whose parent is still running, so only the parent can be signalled

rubric: A zombie is already dead; only its process-table entry remains until the parent reaps it with wait().
Signals cannot remove it; the uninterruptible-sleep explanation describes state D, not Z.

items.prompt: File `a.txt` has a hard link `b.txt` and a symlink `c.txt` pointing to `a.txt`. After `rm a.txt`, `b.txt` still reads fine but `c.txt` fails. Why?

options.label: Removing a name always breaks symlinks first, while hard links are protected by the file's permission bits
The hard link is another name for the same inode, while the symlink stores only the path `a.txt`
The hard link keeps a private copy of the data made at creation, while the symlink only points back at the original
Symlinks are cached in memory and expire when the target is deleted, while hard links are written back to disk

rubric: Both hard links are directory entries for one inode, which survives until its link count reaches zero; a symlink stores a path that now dangles.
The strongest distractor treats hard links as copies, which they are not.

items.prompt: A high-priority task blocks on a mutex held by a low-priority task. Medium-priority tasks keep the CPU, and the high-priority task misses its deadlines. What is the underlying cause?

options.label: The high task spins instead of sleeping, which burns its own quantum and lowers its dynamic priority
The mutex is unfair, so the high task is repeatedly overtaken by newly arriving threads in the wait queue
Medium tasks preempt the low-priority holder, so it cannot run to release the mutex the high task needs
Priorities are ignored while any mutex is held, so all tasks run round robin until the lock is freed

rubric: This is priority inversion: the lock holder is starved by medium tasks, so the high task waits indefinitely.
Distractors blame queue fairness, global priority suspension or spinning, none of which explains the medium-priority tasks' role.

items.prompt: Why is switching between two threads of the same process usually cheaper than switching between two separate processes? Select all that apply.

options.label: The threads share heap and code, so cache contents stay more useful after the switch
The page tables stay the same, so cached address translations in the TLB need not be discarded
Thread switches skip saving registers, because threads share one set of CPU registers
Thread switches never enter the kernel, because the scheduler runs entirely in user space

rubric: Same address space means no page-table switch or TLB flush, and shared data keeps caches warm.
Each thread has its own registers, and kernel threads are switched by the kernel scheduler.

items.prompt: A Linux host has 1 GB of free RAM and no swap. A C program calls `malloc` for 2 GB and gets a non-NULL pointer. It runs normally for a while, then is killed with SIGKILL while filling the buffer. Which explanation fits best?

options.label: The kernel reserved 2 GB of swap on demand at malloc time, and that swap area filled up during the write loop
malloc failed without reporting it, and the first write through the pointer raised a segmentation fault shown as a kill
malloc quietly returned a 1 GB block, and writes past its end corrupted memory, so the kernel killed the process for it
Overcommit let malloc reserve address space only; frames were assigned on first touch until RAM ran out and the OOM killer fired

rubric: malloc reserves virtual address space; physical frames are allocated lazily on first touch, and when none remain the OOM killer sends SIGKILL.
Distractors confuse overcommit with buffer overflow, on-demand swap, or a segfault, which would be SIGSEGV.

items.prompt: A service runs fast until its working set grows past physical RAM. Then throughput drops 50x, CPU use is near 5%, and the disk is saturated with paging I/O. What best explains this?

options.label: The file system journal is full, so every write waits for a checkpoint before continuing
The scheduler is starving the service because its priority was lowered after heavy CPU use
The TLB is too small, so each address translation needs a full trap into a kernel handler
Resident pages are constantly evicted and refaulted, so the process mostly waits on page-ins

rubric: This is thrashing: the working set exceeds RAM, so pages are evicted and refaulted, leaving the CPU idle while it waits on paging I/O.
Distractors blame scheduling or the journal, which would not produce paging I/O with low CPU use.

items.prompt: On Linux, fork() of a process with 4 GB resident memory usually completes in milliseconds. Which mechanism best explains why it is fast?

options.label: The kernel delays creating the child until it calls exec, so no memory is duplicated
The kernel copies only recently touched parent pages and discards the cold ones
The kernel shares the parent's physical pages and copies a page only when one side writes to it
The child shares the parent's address space entirely, so writes by either are visible to both

rubric: Copy-on-write: page tables are duplicated, pages are marked read-only and shared, and a page is copied only on first write.
Distractors confuse fork with threads (shared address space) or with exec/vfork-style deferral.

items.prompt: A high-priority task blocks on a mutex held by a low-priority task. A medium-priority CPU-bound task keeps the low-priority task from running, so the high-priority task stalls for a long time. Which interaction causes this?

options.label: Lock convoy, because the mutex is granted in FIFO order regardless of task priority
Priority inversion, because the medium task delays the lock holder the high task waits on
Deadlock, because the high and low tasks each hold a resource the other needs
Starvation of the medium task, because the scheduler always prefers the highest priority

rubric: Priority inversion: the medium task indirectly blocks the high task by preempting the lock holder.
Deadlock requires a circular wait, which is absent here; convoy and starvation describe different effects.

items.prompt: An application calls write() on a file and gets a success return. The machine loses power a second later, and the data is missing after reboot. What is the most likely cause?

options.label: write() returned early because the file system had already detected a full disk
The kernel dropped the buffer at process exit, because the file descriptors were never closed
The file's inode was locked by another process, so the write was queued and then lost
The data sat in the page cache and was never flushed to the device, since no fsync was issued

rubric: A successful write() only means the data reached the page cache; durability needs fsync or equivalent.
Distractors invent error paths; a full disk would make write() fail, and exit does not discard dirty cache pages.

items.prompt: A loop sums a large in-RAM array by reading one byte per 4096-byte page, repeatedly, and runs far slower per byte than a sequential scan. perf shows no major page faults. Which explanation fits best?

options.label: Each access triggers a minor fault into the kernel, which must zero a freshly allocated page before the read can complete
The scheduler preempts the process more often when it touches memory sparsely, so context switches dominate the runtime
Strided reads bypass the page table, so hardware must consult the file system per address
Each access lands on a different page, causing many TLB and cache misses even though pages are resident

rubric: Page-sized strides defeat TLB reach and cache-line locality, so translation and memory latency dominate.
Distractors assume kernel traps, scheduler effects or file-system lookups that do not occur for resident pages.

items.prompt: Why is a context switch between two threads of the same process usually cheaper than one between two separate processes? Select all that apply.

options.label: The switch needs no kernel scheduler involvement when the threads are kernel threads
Cached TLB entries for the shared mappings can still be useful afterwards
The address space is unchanged, so no page-table switch is needed
The threads share one register set, so nothing needs to be saved or restored

rubric: Same address space means no page-table swap and TLB entries stay valid, which are the main savings.
Each thread has its own registers, and kernel threads are still scheduled by the kernel.

items.prompt: A Linux server with 8 cores shows a load average of 40, yet top reports the CPUs about 90% idle. Many processes are in state D, and the application reads from an NFS mount that has become unresponsive. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.label: Run queue saturation from CPU-bound tasks waiting for a free core, so the server needs more cores to clear the backlog
Tasks are stuck in uninterruptible I/O waits on the stalled mount, adding to load but using no CPU
Zombie processes are piling up because parents never call wait(), and each one holds a scheduler slot and inflates the load
Memory leaks are forcing heavy swapping, and the time spent waiting on swap I/O is hidden from CPU accounting tools

rubric: On Linux, uninterruptible (D state) sleepers count toward load average even though they use no CPU.
Saturation from CPU-bound tasks would show low idle time; zombies do not occupy run queue slots.

items.prompt: A workstation runs an editor that needs quick response and a long compile. Criteria: interactive tasks respond fast, the compile still progresses, and users do not tune per-task settings. Which scheduling policy fits best?

options.label: First-come-first-served, because it avoids preemption overhead and the compile finishes earliest without being interrupted
Multilevel feedback queue, because short-burst tasks stay high priority while aging prevents starvation of CPU hogs
Shortest-job-first using burst lengths the user declares, because it minimises average waiting time for every task in the queue
Strict static priorities set by the user, because interactive tasks then always outrank batch work and respond immediately

rubric: A feedback queue infers behaviour automatically and ages tasks, meeting all three criteria.
FCFS hurts responsiveness, and SJF and static priorities require manual input or risk starvation.

items.prompt: A database buffer cache uses plain LRU. A nightly report scans a table three times larger than RAM once, and morning queries then run slowly. Criteria: keep hot pages cached, minimal tuning. Which change is best?

options.label: Lock the scanned table in memory with mlock, because pinned pages are never evicted and the scan then cannot displace anything
Switch to FIFO replacement, because it never promotes scanned pages above older entries and so protects older hot pages
Use a scan-resistant policy such as 2Q or segmented LRU so single-touch pages cannot evict hot ones
Add more swap space, because evicted pages can be paged back in cheaply when the morning queries need them

rubric: Scan-resistant policies keep once-touched pages in a probationary area, protecting the hot set.
FIFO still evicts hot pages, and swap or mlock do not address cache pollution.

items.prompt: Two critical sections are contended by 4 threads on 8 cores. Section A updates memory for about 2 µs. Section B holds its lock across a disk read of about 5 ms. Which lock choice is best?

options.label: Spinlock for both, since avoiding context switches always lowers latency
Blocking mutex for A, spinlock for B
Spinlock for A, blocking mutex for B
Blocking mutex for both, since spinning is never acceptable on multicore

rubric: Spinning is cheaper than sleeping for very short holds, but wastes cores over millisecond holds.
The others reverse the choice or apply an absolute rule that ignores hold time.

items.prompt: A key-value store must acknowledge a write only after it is durable, and must exceed 20,000 writes/s on an SSD where fsync costs about 1 ms. Criteria: no acknowledged write lost on power failure. Which design is best?

options.label: Rely on the page cache with a 30-second kernel flush, acknowledging each write immediately
Batch concurrent writes into one log append and one fsync, then acknowledge them all
Call fsync after every write on a single thread, since that gives the strongest guarantee
Open the log with O_NONBLOCK so writes return instantly and flush in the background

rubric: Group commit amortises one fsync over many writes, so it keeps durability and reaches the throughput target.
Per-write fsync caps near 1,000/s; delayed flushing and O_NONBLOCK both risk losing acknowledged data.

items.prompt: A server runs third-party plugins that may crash or corrupt memory. Criteria: a faulty plugin must not take down the server or other plugins, and moderate overhead is acceptable. Which architecture is best?

options.label: Separate processes sharing one writable segment, because it gives isolation at no cost
Separate processes per plugin, because distinct address spaces contain crashes and corruption
Threads behind a global lock, because serialising plugins prevents any memory corruption
Threads in one process, because shared memory makes fault containment automatic

rubric: Process boundaries enforce memory isolation, matching the fault-containment criterion at acceptable cost.
Threads share an address space, and a shared writable segment reintroduces corruption paths.

items.prompt: A process with a 64 GB working set and random access shows high TLB miss rates. Which are valid reasons that 2 MB huge pages are a sound remedy? Select all that apply.

options.label: They remove all page faults, since memory is preallocated at exec time
Each TLB entry covers far more memory, so misses fall
They let the process address more memory than its virtual address space allows
Page tables become smaller and walks shorter, so misses cost less

rubric: Larger pages raise TLB reach and shorten page-table walks, which directly address the miss problem.
Huge pages do not eliminate faults or extend the virtual address space.

items.prompt: A container with a 2 GB cgroup memory limit runs a cache service whose heap briefly spikes to 2.3 GB for a few seconds. Criteria: it must not be OOM-killed, latency spikes under 50 ms are acceptable, and the host has spare RAM. Which option is best?

options.label: Lower the limit to 1.5 GB, so the kernel reclaims page cache earlier and prevents the spike
Raise the limit to about 3 GB, because the spike is bounded and the host has spare memory
Disable the OOM killer on the host, because short spikes are recovered by the kernel on their own
Enable swap for the container, because paging the spike to disk is cheaper than adding memory

rubric: A modest limit increase meets the no-kill criterion with spare RAM and no latency penalty.
Swap risks latency beyond 50 ms, a lower limit makes kills more likely, and disabling OOM can hang the host.

items.prompt: A latency-sensitive server runs 64 threads on 8 cores, and each request holds a shared lock for about 2 microseconds. Criteria: lowest tail latency under contention and no wasted CPU while holders are descheduled. Which lock strategy is best?

options.label: Pure blocking mutex that sleeps at once on contention, since a futex wait and wake costs more than a 2 microsecond hold but keeps CPUs free
Pure spinlock, since a 2 microsecond hold is shorter than a context switch so waiters should spin until the lock frees
Adaptive mutex: spin briefly, then block on a futex, so short holds avoid sleeps and preempted holders do not burn CPU
Spinlock with exponential backoff and pause instructions, which cuts cache-line traffic so spinning waiters waste little CPU

rubric: Adaptive spin-then-block handles short holds cheaply and avoids burning CPU when the holder is preempted.
Pure spinning with 8x oversubscription wastes cycles on preempted holders; user space cannot disable interrupts.

items.prompt: A database engine manages its own buffer pool on a file opened normally, so every page is cached twice (engine and page cache). Criteria: avoid double caching and keep control of write ordering for durability. Which critique of the current design is best?

options.label: Drop fsync once O_DIRECT is on, because direct I/O bypasses the page cache and so always guarantees data reaches stable media in write order
Switch to mmap for all I/O, because the kernel then guarantees write ordering and its page eviction decisions will match what the engine needs
Keep buffered I/O and double the buffer pool, because the page cache evicts clean pages instantly at no cost and so duplicates are harmless
Use O_DIRECT for data I/O and keep fsync for ordering; this removes the duplicate cache but the engine must handle alignment and readahead

rubric: O_DIRECT removes double caching; the engine takes on alignment and readahead and still needs fsync for ordering.
mmap gives the kernel control of writeback order; O_DIRECT alone does not guarantee flush of device caches or metadata.

items.prompt: A fleet of containers shares one host. Criteria: a runaway container must not starve neighbours of memory, and a neighbour's crash must not take the host down. Which policy is best?

options.label: Set per-container cgroup memory limits, so only the offender is reclaimed or OOM-killed within its cgroup
Disable swap and overcommit globally, so allocations fail early and the global OOM killer never needs to run on the host
Raise the offending container's CPU priority with nice, so it finishes sooner and returns its memory to the other containers
Run every container as root with no limits, relying on the kernel to share memory fairly between containers by page-fault rate

rubric: cgroup memory limits scope reclaim and OOM kills to the offender.
Global settings and nice do not bound per-container memory use.

items.prompt: Two designs for a log-writing service: (A) call fsync after every record, (B) group commit, fsync once per batch of up to 5 ms of records. Criteria: no acknowledged record lost on power failure, and maximum throughput. Which judgement is right?

options.label: A only, because fsync cannot be batched safely and each record needs its own flush
A only, because batching lets acknowledged records sit unflushed in the page cache during the 5 ms window
B with acks sent when records enter the batch, since the OS page cache is flushed on power loss
B, with acks sent only after the batch fsync returns, so durability holds and fsync cost is shared

rubric: Group commit preserves durability if acks wait for the fsync, and amortises cost.
Acking before fsync loses data; the page cache is volatile.

items.prompt: A real-time audio thread must meet a 5 ms deadline. It shares a mutex with a low-priority logging thread, and a medium-priority CPU-bound thread is also runnable. Deadlines are occasionally missed. Which critique of the fix 'raise the logger's nice value further' is best?

options.label: It is ideal, because the medium thread is the only real cause and the logger's lock use is irrelevant to the misses
It fixes the problem, since a lower-priority logger is scheduled less often and so holds the lock for less total time
It does not help: this is priority inversion, so use priority inheritance or keep the lock off the audio path
It helps only on multicore, since inversion cannot occur when the threads run in real-time scheduling classes

rubric: The classic inversion: the medium thread starves the lock holder; inheritance or lock avoidance fixes it.
Lowering logger priority worsens its chance to release the lock.

items.prompt: A service forks workers from a parent holding 40 GB of mostly read-only data. Criteria: low startup latency and bounded memory growth. Which judgements of fork with copy-on-write are sound? Select all that apply.

options.label: Pages the children only read remain shared, so memory grows with pages written
Refcount updates in a managed runtime can dirty shared pages and erode the sharing
Copy-on-write means fork duplicates no kernel structures, so cost is constant
Fork cost still grows with page-table size, so very large parents can stall for noticeable time

rubric: Page tables are copied, shared pages stay until written, and runtime metadata writes cause copying.
Fork is not constant-time.

items.prompt: A team debates a CPU scheduler for a mixed workload: interactive shells and long batch jobs on a shared server. Criteria: interactive response under 50 ms, no batch starvation, simple tuning. A proposal is strict static priority with interactive jobs on top. Which is the best evaluation?

options.label: Sound: strict priority guarantees both goals, because batch jobs still run whenever interactive jobs are idle, so they cannot starve on this server
Wrong: interactive jobs need the lowest priority so they cannot hog the CPU, since short bursts finish quickly even when they wait behind batch work
Sound, and aging should be avoided because it always raises context-switch cost above the benefit, which would hurt interactive response
Risky: busy interactive jobs can starve batch work; use weighted fair sharing or aging so both goals are met

rubric: Strict priority can starve low classes; weighted fair sharing or aging meets all criteria.
Interactive jobs at lowest priority would hurt response.

items.prompt: Design a crash-safe update of a config file. Constraints: readers never see a partial file, the old or new version survives a power failure, and it works on a POSIX filesystem. Which procedure meets all constraints?

options.label: Write a temp file in /tmp, fsync the temp file, then rename it over the target file
Write a temp file beside the target, rename it over the target, and skip fsync because rename is atomic
Write a temp file in the same directory, fsync it, rename over the target, then fsync the directory
Truncate the target and write the new contents, then fsync the file and its parent directory

rubric: Same-directory temp, fsync, atomic rename and directory fsync gives atomic, durable replacement.
Truncation exposes partial state; cross-filesystem rename is not atomic; rename without fsync can leave an empty file.

items.prompt: Design a sandbox for untrusted image-conversion code. Constraints: no network access, no access to the host filesystem beyond one input and one output directory, bounded memory and CPU, and a small kernel attack surface. Which design meets all of them?

options.label: A chroot into the input directory, process running as root, with ulimit caps on file size, CPU time and address space
A thread in the main service with a watchdog that kills it after a timeout and a memory quota enforced by the language runtime
Separate process in new network and mount namespaces with bind-mounted dirs, cgroup limits and a seccomp syscall allowlist
A normal child process under an unprivileged user that never calls socket, with the conversion library audited for network code

rubric: Namespaces, cgroups and seccomp cover all constraints including attack surface.
Chroot as root is escapable; trust or threads give no isolation.

items.prompt: Design a fix for a producer-consumer queue that occasionally deadlocks. Constraints: bounded buffer of N slots, multiple producers and consumers, no busy waiting, no lost wakeups. Which design meets all constraints?

options.label: One mutex and one shared condition variable, waiting with an if check, and calling signal once after each put or get
Two counting semaphores for empty and full slots, with buffer indices updated by all threads without any mutex
One mutex with two condition variables (not_full, not_empty), waiting in while-loops that recheck the predicate
A spinlock around the buffer, with callers releasing it and polling in a loop until a slot is free

rubric: Predicate rechecking under a mutex avoids lost wakeups and spurious wakeups without busy waiting.
Semaphores alone leave indices racy; polling is busy waiting.

items.prompt: Design a memory strategy for a 64-bit process that scans a 200 GB file once on a host with 32 GB RAM. Constraints: do not evict other processes' hot pages, keep throughput near disk speed, and avoid copying where possible. Which design meets all constraints?

options.label: Read the file into one 200 GB malloc buffer, letting swap absorb the excess, then process it in place
Read sequentially in large aligned chunks, using posix_fadvise SEQUENTIAL and DONTNEED to drop used pages
mmap the file and touch every page in order with default settings, so the kernel's LRU keeps the newest pages
Use many small random reads with a minimal readahead window, so each request stays cheap and cache use stays low

rubric: Sequential reads with advice limit cache pollution and keep disk throughput.
Others exceed RAM, thrash, or defeat readahead.

items.prompt: A proposed design for a user-space network service runs one blocking thread per connection. Requirement: handle 200,000 mostly idle connections with low memory use and a single machine. Which change completes the design?

options.label: Use an epoll event loop with non-blocking sockets and a small worker pool
Fork a separate process per connection so that no memory is shared between clients
Poll each socket in a loop with sleep calls between passes to cut CPU use
Raise the thread stack size so each connection thread can keep more state

rubric: epoll scales readiness notification to many idle connections cheaply.
Threads or processes per connection cost memory and scheduling overhead.

items.prompt: Design a graceful shutdown for a multi-process daemon. Constraints: in-flight requests finish, no orphaned children, and a hard stop after 30 seconds. Which elements belong in the design? Select all that apply.

options.label: Parent catches SIGTERM and immediately sends SIGKILL to all children so that no child can outlive it and become orphaned
After a 30 second timer, send SIGKILL to remaining children
Parent forwards the signal to children and waits for them with waitpid to reap them
Handle SIGTERM by stopping accepts, then draining in-flight work

rubric: Drain, forward and reap, and a SIGKILL deadline together satisfy all constraints.
Relying on SIGKILL alone abandons in-flight requests.

items.prompt: A team proposes a user-space allocator for a long-running service: per-thread free lists, size classes, and memory is never returned to the OS. Constraints: low contention, bounded fragmentation, and RSS must fall after traffic spikes. The design is missing something. What is it?

options.label: Return fully free spans to the OS with madvise or munmap, and trim per-thread caches
Zero freed blocks at free time so the kernel can reclaim those pages and RSS drops
Use larger size classes so fewer, bigger blocks exist and fragmentation stays bounded
Put one global lock around malloc and free so spans are coalesced in a single place

rubric: Releasing free spans and trimming caches lets RSS fall without adding contention.
A global lock adds contention; zeroing does not return memory.
